extracted.intended_audience: authors, publishers, editors, rights managers, and copyright practitioners (including publishing lawyers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and legal standards on copyright duration, notice, registration, licensing, and common provisions in publishing agreements for books, journal articles, and related works. Focused on practical rules publishers and authors must follow when acquiring, licensing, or administering rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content of the copyright notice
rubrics_metrics.description: The notice consists of three parts: (1) either the symbol ©, or the word Copyright, or the abbreviation Copr.; (2) the year of first publication; and (3) the name of the copyright owner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many publishers also add “all rights reserved” (harmless but largely obsolete). The year of first publication is not needed for greeting cards, postcards, stationery, and certain other works. For works in their renewal term it is customary, but not required, to include the year of renewal as well as the year of first publication. Other admonitions (e.g., prohibitions on reproduction) are not legally necessary but may serve as notices to users.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement of the copyright notice
rubrics_metrics.description: The notice should be placed so as to give reasonable notice of the claim of copyright to the consumer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Traditional placement remains common: for books on the title page or the page immediately following; for journals and magazines on the title page, the first page of text, or the front cover. Publishers generally continue to follow old-law traditional locations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Name used in the notice
rubrics_metrics.description: The name used in the notice should be the name of the author unless the author has assigned all rights to the publisher.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publisher names often appear even when they do not own all rights; authors sometimes insist on notice in their names despite assignment. Such vagaries are usually harmless except when they mislead those seeking permission to use material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice on derivative works
rubrics_metrics.description: A new copyright in a derivative work entitles its publisher to use a new copyright notice with the current year date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nothing requires the notice to delineate what is and is not covered by the copyright; better practice for revised editions is to include publication years of various editions to avoid implying the copyright extends to public-domain material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correcting notice mistakes (retroactive regimes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different remedial rules apply depending on publication date: pre-1978, 1978–Feb 28, 1989, and on/after March 1, 1989.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre-1978 mistakes could cause forfeiture; 1978–1989 a one-year date error or small-number omission could be excused; more serious omissions could be cured by registering within five years and making a “reasonable effort” to add notice to distributed copies. For works first published on or after March 1, 1989, no notice is required, but continued use of notice is strongly advised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deposit requirements to the Library of Congress
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers must send copies of works published in print form to the Copyright Office for deposit in the Library of Congress within three months of publication; two copies of the 'best edition' are required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to deposit does not forfeit copyright but can result in fines if a specific request is ignored. For simultaneous cloth and paperback, send two cloth copies; expensive or limited editions may apply to submit one copy. Electronic publications currently have different deposit rules (single copy options), and foreign-distributed works are subject to deposit requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Registration forms and group-registration rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Registration is done ordinarily via the Copyright Office’s interactive online application; paper forms are still available and are required for certain group registrations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paper forms slow registration and are mandatory for group registrations (multiple photographs, unpublished works, contributions to periodicals by a single author). Fees vary by process; registrants with many titles may keep deposit accounts at the Copyright Office. The Office provides tutorials and explanations online.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for accuracy and candor in registration
rubrics_metrics.description: All questions on the registration application must be answered accurately; statements do not have to be exhaustive but must be correct and not evasive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have sanctioned copyright owners for misleading the Copyright Office (e.g., failing to disclose that a work is based on preexisting materials). Unlike patent applications, there is no general duty to disclose adverse claims beyond what the form asks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benefits of registration
rubrics_metrics.description: Registration is not necessary to obtain copyright but confers important procedural and substantive benefits in enforcement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Registration (especially within three months of publication or before infringement) is a prerequisite to bring suit (with some foreign-work exceptions), allows recovery of statutory damages and attorney’s fees, and avoids later scrambling to register. The Copyright Office also offers a preregistration procedure for works at risk of prepublication piracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration — 'life plus seventy' default rule (post-1977 works)
rubrics_metrics.description: For works created after 1977 the paradigmatic term is the life of the author plus seventy years; for joint works, life of last to die plus 70.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the general rule but many exceptions apply (see works made for hire, anonymous/pseudonymous works, and special media rules). Works existing before 1978 may be governed by special transitional rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration for works made for hire
rubrics_metrics.description: For works made for hire the term is ninety-five years from first publication or 120 years from creation, whichever expires first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the owner is not the actual creator (often a corporate entity), a fixed-term rule applies rather than life-plus-seventy. The termination right generally does not apply to works made for hire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration for anonymous and pseudonymous works
rubrics_metrics.description: Anonymous and pseudonymous works are given the same fixed term as works made for hire—95 years from first publication or 120 years from creation—unless the author’s identity is filed with the Copyright Office, in which case life-plus-seventy may apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing the author’s identity with the Copyright Office shifts the term back to the ordinary life-plus-seventy rule (unless the work is made for hire).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-1978 unpublished works transitional protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre-1978 unpublished works that were still under common-law copyright when the 1978 law took effect receive transitional protection: at least until December 31, 2002, and if published before December 31, 2002, protected at least until December 31, 2047.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This prevents late-published works from becoming immediately public-domain under the new regime; these works thus have meaningful minimum terms under the transition rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-1978 works published in the United States (renewal rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Works published in the U.S. before January 1, 1923 are in the public domain; works published 1923–1963 have a 95-year term from first publication only if copyright was properly renewed in the 28th year; works published 1964–1977 are protected for 95 years from first publication because renewal is automatic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determining renewal status often requires searching Copyright Office renewal records. The above assumes proper copyright notice was used at all times; failure of notice can change results.

rubrics_metrics.name: New copyright for new or materially modified editions
rubrics_metrics.description: Each time a work is materially modified a new copyright arises covering the new or revised material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus republishing an earlier public-domain edition may be legal, but a later revision (e.g., a 1934 revision of a 1920 treatise) might still be under copyright, making republication of the later version restricted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-1978 works first published abroad and restoration rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress restored copyright (effective January 1, 1996) to many foreign works that had forfeited U.S. copyright for failure to comply with notice/renewal formalities, subject to certain protections for parties who relied on apparent forfeiture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restored copyrights are subject to complex conditions. Ninth Circuit precedent creates an anomaly: non-U.S. works published abroad before 1923 may still be eligible for U.S. copyright if no effort was made at the time to comply with U.S. rules (a rule applicable within the Ninth Circuit).

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility for restoration specific criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: A work is eligible for restoration if it was first published outside the United States and if at least one author was not a U.S. citizen or domiciled in the U.S.; an exception exists for works published in the U.S. within thirty days after publication abroad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works published in the U.S. within thirty days after foreign publication to secure Berne-like treatment are excluded from restoration eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection of Copyright Management Information (CMI)
rubrics_metrics.description: The law prevents intentional removal or alteration of copyright management information, or deliberate use of false CMI, if done with intent to induce, enable, facilitate, or conceal infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This creates liability for tampering with metadata or notices intended to identify ownership or terms; it is a separate layer of legal protection beyond copyright itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademark protection of titles and elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Copying only the title of a work would likely not be copyright infringement, but a title may acquire trademark protection under federal or state law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Book titles are harder to protect than journal or lecture titles due to judicial reluctance to give trademark protection to names used on only a single product; however, some titles (e.g., Gone with the Wind, Winnie-the-Pooh) can be protectable, and franchising can extend trademark protection beyond copyright duration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic versus subsidiary rights (the 'bundle' concept)
rubrics_metrics.description: Copyright is a bundle of basic rights (reproduce, distribute, make derivative works, perform/display publicly) and subsidiary rights (rights for other languages, audio, motion picture, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each right can be separately licensed or assigned and subdivided by geography, time, or medium. Publishers often administer subsidiary rights or license them to third parties; exploiting subsidiary rights effectively is a publisher responsibility to the author.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author retention and licensing of subsidiary rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors (especially trade-book authors with agents) may retain some or all subsidiary rights and license them directly; however, permissions are typically still handled by the publisher.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where authors retain rights, licensing to foreign publishers, motion-picture producers, etc. is often handled via the author's agent; when publishers are part of conglomerates they may license intramurally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uses of public-domain works and derivative-work limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Once a work is in the public domain, it is free for all to use; derivative works are entitled to copyright only in their new material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determining public-domain status requires careful attention to complex statutory and historical rules; markets outside the United States may remain closed if foreign terms differ from U.S. status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subdividing a copyright (carving by territory, time, medium)
rubrics_metrics.description: A copyright can be subdivided so that different parties control rights by geography, time period, or medium (e.g., Publisher A gets North American rights, Publisher B UK rights; hardcover vs paperback; French translation license for ten years).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is theoretically wide latitude in how rights are carved up, limited only by market demand and parties' creativity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusive versus nonexclusive licenses
rubrics_metrics.description: Licenses may be exclusive or nonexclusive; exclusive licensees are treated like owners of copyright and generally have standing to sue, while nonexclusive licensees hold a personal privilege and typically cannot sue or transfer the license without permission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have cast some doubt on presumed assignability of exclusive licenses; drafters should expressly state assign/sublicense rights. Parties making substantial investments usually insist on exclusivity; ephemeral users generally accept nonexclusive rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Goals of licensors and licensees; scope drafting guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: In drafting copyright licenses, the parties must define the scope of the license clearly, taking into account possible evolution of technologies and markets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Licensors want narrow definitions to preserve future flexibility; licensees want broad rights. Both need clarity and understandability. Drafting licenses requires skillful negotiation and good communication between lawyers and clients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Payment terms and effect of nonpayment
rubrics_metrics.description: A license and the obligation to pay are usually treated as reciprocal obligations; failure to pay royalties does not automatically terminate the license and convert the licensee into an infringer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nonpayment typically gives the licensor contract damages rather than a copyright infringement claim; shrewd licensors will try to make timely payment a condition of the validity of the license, and shrewd licensees will resist such a condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Termination of transfers and licenses (contractual and statutory)
rubrics_metrics.description: Contracts may include express termination provisions (e.g., out-of-print clauses, sales thresholds). Statutorily, authors and their families may terminate post-1977 copyright arrangements after thirty-five years (with comparable rules for pre-1978 grants), though termination does not apply to works made for hire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drafting out-of-print clauses is complicated by digital editions and print-on-demand. Mechanics of statutory termination (who may terminate, procedures) are complex and require careful attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common book-contract provisions to negotiate
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical negotiated areas include: royalty rates and escalation; royalty advances and expense allowances; standards for acceptance of manuscript and publisher’s discretion to terminate if manuscript is not 'satisfactory'; period after acceptance within which publisher must issue the work; what rights (beyond home-territory print rights) and digital rights are granted; indemnification obligations; scope of noncompete; share of royalties for revised editions the author did not contribute to; reversion conditions if out of print; audit rights; exact specification of Creative Commons or open-access terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These contract terms determine economic and control outcomes for authors and publishers. For indemnification, when publisher carries 'media perils' insurance, indemnity obligations are often negotiated with reference to coverage. Option clauses (rights of first review/refusal or matching) and other special agreements (journal-article transfers, collective-work contributions, works made for hire forms for translations/forewords/indexes) are also common and must be tailored to the work type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Option clauses and rights on subsequent works
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishing agreements may include options on the author’s next book, rights of first review or first refusal, or rights to match outstanding offers on the author’s next book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such clauses are less common today than historically, but are more prevalent where books are part of a series or set of related titles. The exact scope of an option (by subject, character, or other delimitation) is a material point of negotiation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical provisions for journal-article and contributed-chapter agreements
rubrics_metrics.description: Journal-article agreements often transfer all copyright rights to the publisher while sometimes transferring limited rights back to the author (e.g., right to reprint in scholarly contexts); agreements for contributions to collective works set out transfer/consent terms and differ from 'works made for hire' forms used for translations, forewords, or indexes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forms vary by publisher; contributors should review whether rights to reuse, reprint, post on repositories, or include in author collections are reserved or transferred. Special forms are used when the contribution is commissioned or constitutes a work made for hire.
